meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'чему').

examples.text: Почему вы лезете на мою кухню?
examples.trans: Why are you meddling in my kitchen?
Then why did she lie to me?
Why are we going so slowly?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'you (polite/plural)', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: This is our new head chef.
He fired the best cooks in Moscow.
You look simply like a princess.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'push in, barge in', paired with 'полезть'.

examples.text: Почему вы лезете на мою кухню?
examples.trans: Why are you meddling in my kitchen?
Don't jump the queue!
The cat is climbing the tree.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'on, onto', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: С возвращением тебя к нам, Витя!
examples.trans: Welcome back to us, Vitya!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'my', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Did you understand me, my friend?
Because this is my restaurant.
He is my very best friend.

meanings.note: Entered Russian via Polish 'kuchnia' and Middle High German 'küchen', ultimately from Late Latin 'coquina' (from 'coquere', to cook).

examples.trans: Let us go to the kitchen quickly.
Only the best work in the kitchen!
Show them who is the master in the kitchen.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'тому').

examples.trans: Because this is my restaurant.

examples.text: Потому что я повар. Я настоящий профессионал.
examples.trans: Because I am a cook. I am a true professional.
Because I am a cook.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what, that', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I do, and what does that mean?
Nastya, tell me, what should I do?
Wait, have we arrived already?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'this, it (is)', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: That title will be his in twenty-four hours.
This is our new head chef.
Really, and who is this man?

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'restaurant' (from 'restaurer', to restore strength with rich broth); entered Russian in the early 19th century.

examples.trans: And change the name of the restaurant altogether!
Because this is my restaurant.
I am not worried about the restaurant.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: С возвращением тебя к нам, Витя!
examples.trans: Welcome back to us, Vitya!
Misha, thank you for everything.
And thank you all very much.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'егодня').

examples.trans: Let us hold a fair duel today.
Let us leave here together today.
Chef, we will tear them apart today!

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'вадьба'). Common feminine noun meaning 'wedding' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: На свадьбе я буду не одна.
examples.trans: At the wedding I will not be alone.
I will definitely introduce you at the wedding.
Before the wedding you must not see me.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'of (my) daughter' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: See you very soon, daughter!
And today is my daughter's wedding.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'I', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Welcome back to us, Vitya!

examples.text: Папа, он пока ещё не зять.
examples.trans: Dad, he is not your son-in-law yet.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'will be'.

examples.text: Как это может быть не он?
examples.trans: How could it not be him?
I have a toy car.
Childhood was hard.

meanings.en: to supervise, to keep an eye on, to control
meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to control / supervise', paired with 'проконтролировать'.

examples.trans: I will supervise every dish.
I'm supposed to keep an eye on you!
Keep an eye on me right here!

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('every, each').

examples.trans: Each pair will prepare one dish.
I will supervise every dish.
Check the plating of every dish yourself!

meanings.note: Common neuter noun meaning 'dish' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Each pair will prepare one dish.
Chef, forgive me for the dish.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: Clear enough, then supervise it here yourself.

examples.text: Я никого пытать не буду, ясно?
examples.trans: I'm not going to torture anyone, got it?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'then', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Then take away my signature menu!

Clear enough, then supervise it here yourself.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'ourselves', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Anywhere at all, choose for yourself.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'here', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Vitya, wait here for a minute.
Do not drink too much here.

examples.text: Я тут ночью к тебе заходил.
examples.trans: I stopped by here at night.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'further, on', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Keep supervising, respected maestro!
All right. Next.
What's next?

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'важаемый'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('esteemed, respected').

examples.trans: Keep supervising, respected maestro!
Esteemed veteran, listen to me.

meanings.note: Common neuter noun meaning 'maestro' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Keep supervising, respected maestro!

examples.text: На кухне отеля всегда есть маэстро.
examples.trans: In the hotel kitchen there is always maestro.

meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'верять'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to check, test, verify', paired with 'проверить'.

examples.trans: Check the plating of every dish yourself!
He is testing us.
The teacher is checking notebooks.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'дача'). Common feminine noun meaning 'serving / plating' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Check the plating of every dish yourself!
The dish is completely ready for serving.

examples.text: Вот этот заказ готов к подаче.
examples.trans: This order is ready to serve.

meanings.note: Prefix 'во-' ('into, up') marks inward or upward movement (stem 'обще').

examples.trans: And change the name of the restaurant altogether!
I do not remember anything at all.

meanings.en: to do, to get up to (something outrageous)
meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'are doing, perpetrating', paired with 'сотворить'.

examples.trans: What on earth are you doing in here?

examples.text: Он сам не понимает, что творит.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'all', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: You have a real circus in here!

meanings.note: Common neuter noun meaning 'good, welcome' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Thank you for the kind words.

meanings.en: to come, arrive (idiomatic in добро пожаловать = welcome)

examples.trans: Welcome to this kitchen.

meanings.en: to leave, to go away (on foot)

examples.trans: Guys, let us leave quickly, follow me!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'for', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I just advised adding salt!

examples.trans: I just advised adding salt!
